Read Before Write

Checking a row exists before updating or deleting it, so a missing id becomes a clean 404, not a raw Prisma error.

prisma.tag.update({ where: { id } }) against an id that doesn't exist doesn't quietly do nothing — it throws (Prisma's P2025, "record not found"). Left alone, that throw would still reach the client as a 500, or now, after the previous topic's error-handler work, a 404 — but a fairly blunt one, without a chance to name which resource wasn't found the way getTicketById's existing ApiError(404, 'Ticket 5 not found') already does.

Every update and delete controller in this project takes the simpler route instead: check the row exists first, with the same getById the GET route already uses, before ever calling update/delete on it.

// Figure 3.9: checking existence before writing (src/controllers/tag.controller.js, excerpt)
export const updateTag = asyncHandler(async (req, res) => {
  const existing = await tagService.getTagById(req.params.id);

  if (!existing) {
    throw new ApiError(404, `Tag ${req.params.id} not found`);
  }

  const tag = await tagService.updateTag(req.params.id, req.body);
  sendResource(res, tag);
});

This costs one extra query — getTagById runs, then updateTag runs again right after — which is a deliberate trade, not an oversight: the resulting 404 names exactly what wasn't found, in the exact same shape as every other 404 in this API, and the code reads as two plain, sequential steps rather than a try/catch decoding why Prisma's own error was thrown. ticket.controller.js and comment.controller.js follow the identical shape for their own update/delete functions.
